chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr ibn Suwayd from Yahya al-Halabi from Mu' from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): It was mentioned to us that a man from the Ansar died while he owed two dinars, so the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) did not pray over him, and he said, 'Pray over your companion,' until some of his relatives guaranteed them for him.

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said, 'That is correct.' Then he (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) only did that so that they would take heed, and so that one would call the other to account, and so that they would not轻视 the debt. And indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) died while he had a debt, and Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) died while he had a debt, and Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) was killed while he had a debt.'

key_terms.لِيَتَّعِظُوا: So that they would take heed/be admonished

ai.seo_question: Why did the Prophet withhold the funeral prayer from the man who died with debt, and did the Imams also have debts?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* to clarify the juristic ruling that unpaid debt does not prevent the performance of funeral prayers, but rather serves as a pedagogical tool to ensure financial accountability. The Imam highlights the continuity of this practice among the Ahl al-Bayt, noting that the Prophet, Imam Hasan, and Imam Husayn all died with outstanding debts, thereby establishing that debt is a civil obligation separate from spiritual status. This context reinforces the Shia scholarly view that the Prophet's withholding of the prayer was a deliberate lesson to prevent the community from neglecting creditors, rather than a punishment for the deceased.
